The Capital Markets Authority has approved a Short Form Prospectus allowing eligible Kenyan investors to participate in the Dangote Petroleum Refinery & Petrochemicals IPO through Global Depositary Receipts (GDRs).

Renaissance Capital Kenya will aggregate local investor funds, work with Renaissance Capital Africa in Nigeria and structure GDRs after allocation of the underlying shares.

The GDRs are intended for listing on the NSE, subject to Nigeria SEC approval, a successful fund raise and share allocation.

CMA said the transaction is the first of its kind under Kenya’s GDR framework and clarified that the offer does not include Dangote’s planned Lamu refinery.

Kenya’s Eurobond yields have surged sharply in recent days as a global government bond selloff spills into frontier markets.

◉ The 2032 yield jumped 109 basis points to 8.752% between September 22 and October 1, while the 2034 rose 107 bps to 9.202%.

◉ The 2028 climbed 95 bps to 7.626%, with yields rising as bond prices fell.

The selloff comes as the benchmark U.S. 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.34%, its highest since 2002, amid renewed inflation, interest-rate and government debt concerns.

Higher global yields could complicate Kenya’s planned US$815Mn Eurobond issuance in October-December, increasing the return investors may demand on new borrowing.

Kenyan investors could gain access to the Dangote Petroleum Refinery IPO through a proposed Global Depositary Receipt (GDR) listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange, subject to final CMA and NSE approvals.

➠ 1. Kenyan investors apply through licensed local brokers.
➠ 2. Brokers collect orders and complete KYC requirements.
➠ 3. Renaissance Capital Kenya aggregates the applications.
➠ 4. Renaissance Capital Nigeria submits the combined order into the Dangote Refinery IPO.
➠ 5. Underlying shares are allotted in Nigeria through the NGX offer.
➠ 6. Stanbic Bank holds the underlying shares in custody.
➠ 7. GDRs are issued in Kenya against those Nigerian shares.
➠ 8. The GDRs list on the NSE and trade in Kenyan shillings.
➠ 9. CDSC settles the trades and credits investors’ CDS accounts.

Target NSE listing: 8 December 2026, subject to CMA and NSE approval.

Uganda has approved the distribution of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals FZE’s Nigerian IPO to eligible local investors, extending the offer’s reach into East Africa after Kenya cleared a separate access route.

CMA Uganda said the offer may only be marketed through licensed intermediaries that receive its written no-objection, with promotion restricted to high-net-worth individuals and professional investors.

Mass solicitation to the general public is prohibited. The application was submitted by Stanbic IBTC Capital on behalf of Dangote, while Nigeria’s SEC had already approved the underlying IPO.

Kenya, meanwhile, has cleared investor participation through approved intermediaries and an NSE-linked GDR structure, giving Dangote two distinct regional distribution channels.

Uganda’s Capital Markets Authority has restricted local participation in Dangote Petroleum Refinery’s IPO to high-net-worth individuals and professional investors, barring mass marketing to the general public.

Eligible investors must access the offer through CMA-licensed intermediaries that have separately received the regulator’s written no-objection.

CMA said its approval covers distribution of the Nigerian IPO in Uganda and does not amount to an endorsement of the investment or its expected returns.

Turaco appoints Cedrick Todwell as Chief Commercial Officer, Africa, to oversee commercial strategy, partnerships, and market expansion across Africa.

The microinsurance company, which operates in Kenya, Uganda, Nigeria, Ghana, Zambia, and Tanzania, has reached over eight million people through embedded partnerships with firms including M-KOPA, Safaricom, Absa, Airtel, and Moniepoint.

Turaco entered Pakistan in 2026 and plans to launch in two additional African underwriting markets by year end. The company ranked 29th among Africa’s fastest-growing companies in the FT 2026 ranking and second among Kenyan companies.

Dangote’s Kenyan GDR offer targets KSh 39Bn through up to 728.97Mn receipts priced at KSh 53.50 each, with every GDR representing one underlying Dangote Refinery share offered in Nigeria at ₦525.

The minimum application is 2,000 GDRs, or KSh 107,000, with additional subscriptions in multiples of 100.

The offer price reflects the underlying share price, foreign-exchange conversion and GDR expenses.

The GDR operates as a pass-through vehicle, meaning dividends and other corporate actions on the underlying shares flow to Kenyan holders; cash dividends paid in naira or US dollars will be converted into shillings, net of fees and applicable withholding taxes.

The KSh 39Bn size is a target and depends on the final allocation of underlying IPO shares.

Kenyan investors can subscribe directly to the Dangote Petroleum Refinery IPO through Ecobank Transactional Incorporated and SBG Securities, which the Nigerian prospectus names as African distribution channels for investors outside Nigeria.

The route allows eligible Kenyan investors to apply for the underlying DPRP shares at the ₦525 IPO price, with applications generally starting from a minimum of 10 shares and thereafter in multiples of 10.

It sits alongside the separate KSh 39Bn NSE GDR structure, under which each KSh 53.50 GDR represents one DPRP share and gives investors access through a locally listed, Kenya-based custody and settlement framework.

The Central Bank of Kenya has held the CBR at 8.75% for a fourth consecutive meeting, saying the current stance remains appropriate to keep inflation expectations anchored and the exchange rate stable.

September inflation rose to 6.8% from 6.6%, while core inflation increased to 4.0% from 3.4%. CBK raised its 2026 GDP growth forecast to 5.0% from 4.9%, with 2027 growth retained at 5.3%.

Private-sector credit growth strengthened to 10.6% in September, while average lending rates stood at 14.4%. The current account deficit is projected at 3.2% of GDP in 2026, with FX reserves at US$14.70Bn, equivalent to 5.9 months of import cover.

CBK said it will continue monitoring global oil prices, second-round inflation effects and wider domestic and global developments, and stands ready to act if necessary.

The banking sector’s gross non-performing loan ratio fell to 13.9% in September 2026, dropping below 14% for the first time since December 2022.

The ratio improved from 14.8% in June 2026 and 17.6% in August 2025, a decline of 370 basis points from last year’s peak.

CBK said lower NPLs were recorded in the financial services, agriculture, trade, and energy and water sectors, while banks continued to maintain adequate provisions.

The regulator said the banking sector remains stable and resilient, supported by strong liquidity and capital adequacy ratios.

Kenyan fintech Cloud9, founded by former Marketforce Tesh Mbaabu, has raised $500,000 from New York-based accelerator Alliance, taking its disclosed funding to $1 million.

The money will go toward expanding payment corridors, launching virtual and physical cards, and acquiring customers. Cloud9 lets users hold shillings, dollars, euros, pounds and yuan, and settles cross-border payments with stablecoins USDC and USDT, so a Nairobi merchant can pay a supplier in Guangzhou without relying on correspondent banks.

The company says it has opened more than 25,000 accounts since launching, with transaction volumes growing over 15% week over week.

Kenya Airways (KQ) has confirmed government approval of a US$350Mn (KSh 45.15Bn) shareholder loan with a proposed 10-year tenor.

The government may convert the loan into equity, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals, or agree on early repayment. The financing will cover aircraft maintenance, returning grounded aircraft to service and other urgent operating needs.

KQ also confirmed in-principle approval to convert approximately KSh 122Bn in existing government loans, plus accrued interest, into an equity-qualifying tradable instrument. The restructuring aims to restore positive equity and support a capital raise through an Investment Memorandum.

KQ urged caution when trading its shares until the terms and required approvals are finalised.

Ethiopia's largest private lender, Awash Bank, has launched five Mastercard products targeting individual and corporate customers, expanding access to international payments following foreign exchange reforms.

The portfolio includes World Elite debit, Platinum and Gold prepaid, corporate prepaid and domestic contactless cards, alongside a virtual prepaid option.

Awash said its existing international prepaid cards served over 20,000 customers, processing more than US$55Mn in completed transactions during the last financial year, against US$60Mn authorised.

The bank serves over 17Mn customers through more than 1,010 branches, with 4Mn card users and 5Mn Awash Birr Pro users.

The launch builds on its Mastercard partnership established in 2024.

Microsoft’s Africa Development Centre in Nairobi is facing closure, raising concerns about the future of Kenya’s technology workforce.

The development comes amid Microsoft’s global restructuring, which has affected its Kenyan engineering operations.

ICT Cabinet Secretary William Kabogo has called for the protection of local jobs, while Microsoft says it remains committed to serving customers in Kenya and across the region.

Kenya Power was owed Ksh41.5 billion in unpaid bills by postpaid customers at the end of June 2026, nearly Ksh2.5 billion more than a year earlier, with nearly Ksh8 billion owed by public institutions and Ksh33.56 billion by households and private businesses.

About Ksh20.4 billion has been unpaid for more than three months, pushing the utility's provision for potentially irrecoverable bills to Ksh14.89 billion.

The government also owes a separate Ksh35 billion under the Rural Electrification Scheme, even as Kenya Power posted a net profit of Ksh24.9 billion in the last financial year.
